mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Mama ‌Quilla ​place moon, ​marriage ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### Origins ‌(Myth)

​Mama ‌Quilla appears ​in ‌incan tradition ​as ​moon, ​marriage. The ​name's ​meaning, "Mother ‌moon", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about this ​figure.

### ‌Worship ​and Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Mama ‌Quilla ​in ritual, ​text, ‌and ​iconography, ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The ​myths of ​Mama ​Quilla survive ​in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so that ​readers ‌can ​compare them. ‌The ​restoration Mama ‌Quilla ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

‌Were ​such evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Mama ‌Quilla, sanctuary ​or ‌cult ​remains ​tied ​to ‌moon and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes ​(name and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Mama ​Quilla** (*mamaquilla*) ‌— ‌Moon, Marriage ​· ​Mother moon ​— ​belongs to ​the ‌Incan tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Moon, ​Marriage". ‌The name ​means ​"Mother moon"[^1].

​**Mama ​Quilla** — ​**Mother ‌Moon** — ​is ‌the Inca ​goddess ‌of the ​moon, ‌**sister and ​wife ‌of the ​Sun, ​mother of ‌the dynasty's ‌founders, ‌and keeper ​of ​the calendar**. ‌Silver ​was her ​metal, ‌the night ​her ​realm, and ‌the ​Coya — ‌the ​queen — ​her ​living image ​on ‌earth.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records ​the canonical ‌scholarly ​spelling **Mama ​Quilla** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/mamaquilla/). ​The ‌displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*mamaquilla* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered diacritics ‌or ​special encoding ‌is ‌claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for ​this name; ​**Mama ​Quilla** is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken form. ‌Etymologically the ​name ‌means "Mother ​moon"[^1].

The ‌canonical ​spelling **Mama ​Quilla** ​matches the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form *mamaquilla* ​contains the ‌same ​letters, so ‌no ​lost diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ​is claimed. ‌The editorial ‌work ‌is to ​fix ​one reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ​the original ‌evidence ​visible. The ‌displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ‌from the ‌displayed ​form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **m** ‌→ ‌**M** — ‌Same, capitalized
- ‌**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- **m** ​→ **m** ​— ‌Same

meditation.body: Mama ​Quilla embodies ‌the ‌Andean genius ​for **pairing**. ​The ​Inca universe ​is ​built of ‌twinned powers ​— ​sun and ‌moon, ​gold and ‌silver, ​hanan and ‌hurin, emperor ​and ​Coya — ​and ​she is ​the ‌night half ​of the ‌founding ​pair. Where ‌the ​sun commands, ‌the moon ​counts: ‌her office ​is ​time, the ‌patient ‌arithmetic of ‌waxing and ​waning ​by which ‌planting, ​festival, and ​warfare ‌were scheduled. ​That the ​dynasty's ‌mother is ​the ‌*moon* rather ​than the ​sun ​is a ​quiet ‌but profound ‌statement: ​empire's light ‌may blaze, ​but ​its continuity ‌— ‌months, gestations, ‌harvests ‌— is ​feminine and ‌lunar. ​Her eclipse ​myth ​sharpens the ‌point: the ​moon's ​darkness is ​the ‌moment the ​whole ​community must ​shout. A ‌civilization, ​the goddess ‌suggests, ​is measured ‌not ​by its ‌triumphs but ‌by ​whether it ​makes ​noise for ​its mother ‌when ‌she is ​attacked.[^1]
